prompt: An IR spectrum has no absorptions at 3300 or 2150 cm^−1. What can you conclude?

choices.text: The compound is not a terminal alkyne
The compound is not an alcohol
choices.why: An alcohol is ruled out by having no absorption near 3400 cm^−1.

choices.text: The compound must be a simple alkane
choices.why: Missing bands rule out particular groups; they don't prove what the compound is.

choices.text: The compound is not a ketone
choices.why: A ketone is ruled out by having no strong C=O band in the carbonyl range, 1670–1780 cm^−1.

explanation: You can also get structural information from absorptions that are not present. If a spectrum has no absorptions at 3300 and 2150 cm^−1, the compound is not a terminal alkyne; if it has no absorption near 3400 cm^−1, the compound is not an alcohol.

prompt: Why is the IR spectrum of an alkane fairly uninformative?

choices.text: It has only C–H and C–C bands, which most organic compounds share
Alkanes don't absorb infrared radiation between 4000 and 400 cm^−1
choices.why: Alkane C–H bonds absorb strongly from 2850 to 2960 cm^−1, and C–C bonds show bands from 800 to 1300 cm^−1.

choices.text: All of its absorptions lie above 4000 cm^−1, out of range
choices.why: Alkane bands fall inside the usual range: 2850–2960 cm^−1 for C–H and 800–1300 cm^−1 for C–C.

choices.text: Its C–H stretching bands are much too weak to be seen
choices.why: Alkane C–H bonds show a strong absorption from 2850 to 2960 cm^−1.

explanation: The IR spectrum of an alkane is fairly uninformative because no functional groups are present: all absorptions are due to C–H bonds (strong, 2850–2960 cm^−1) and C–C bonds (800–1300 cm^−1). Since most organic compounds contain saturated alkane-like portions, most have these absorptions too.

prompt: Why can the C=C absorption of some alkenes be hard to see?

choices.text: It can be small when the alkene is symmetric
It is hidden under the broad O–H band
choices.why: Alkene C=C bonds absorb near 1650 cm^−1, far from the O–H region at 3400–3650 cm^−1.

choices.text: It lies below 400 cm^−1, outside the usual range
choices.why: Alkene C=C bonds usually absorb near 1650 cm^−1.

choices.text: Only terminal alkenes have a C=C bond that can stretch
choices.why: Every alkene has a C=C bond; symmetric ones just give a small peak.

explanation: Alkene C=C bonds usually absorb near 1650 cm^−1, although in some cases their peaks can be rather small and difficult to see clearly when the alkene is symmetric, or nearly so.

prompt: Which IR absorptions let you work out the substitution pattern on a carbon–carbon double bond?

choices.text: =C–H out-of-plane bending bands at 700–1000 cm^−1
=C–H stretching bands at 3020–3100 cm^−1
choices.why: That stretch shows that a vinylic C–H is present. The substitution pattern comes from the out-of-plane bending bands.

choices.text: The C=C stretching band near 1650 cm^−1
choices.why: The C=C stretch shows a double bond is present; the section uses the =C–H out-of-plane bending bands for the substitution pattern.

choices.text: Alkane C–H stretching bands at 2850–2960 cm^−1
choices.why: Those come from the saturated, alkane-like parts of the molecule.

explanation: Alkenes have characteristic =C–H out-of-plane bending absorptions in the 700 to 1000 cm^−1 range, which allow the substitution pattern on a double bond to be determined.

prompt: An alkene shows strong bands at 910 and 990 cm^−1. What does this suggest about its double bond?

choices.text: It is monosubstituted, like 1-hexene
It is 1,1-disubstituted, R2C=CH2
choices.why: 1,1-Disubstituted alkenes show a single intense band at a different position, not this pair.

choices.text: It has no vinylic hydrogens
choices.why: These are =C–H out-of-plane bending bands, so the double bond must carry vinylic hydrogens.

choices.text: Nothing, since bands below 1500 cm^−1 carry no structural information
choices.why: The =C–H out-of-plane bending bands at 700–1000 cm^−1 reveal the substitution pattern of the double bond.

explanation: Alkene =C–H out-of-plane bending absorptions at 700–1000 cm^−1 reveal the substitution pattern. Monosubstituted alkenes such as 1-hexene show strong characteristic bands at 910 and 990 cm^−1.

prompt: 1,1-Disubstituted alkenes, R2C=CH2, show an intense =C–H out-of-plane bending band at what wavenumber?
explanation: 1,1-Disubstituted alkenes (R2C=CH2) have an intense band at 890 cm^−1, while monosubstituted alkenes such as 1-hexene show strong bands at 910 and 990 cm^−1.

prompt: How does the C≡C stretching absorption of a terminal alkyne compare with that of an internal alkyne?

choices.text: It is much more intense
It is much less intense
choices.why: That is reversed: the C≡C absorption is much more intense for terminal alkynes.

choices.text: It appears near 1650 cm^−1 instead of at 2100–2260 cm^−1
choices.why: Both kinds of alkyne absorb at 2100–2260 cm^−1. 1650 cm^−1 is an alkene C=C.

choices.text: Only internal alkynes show a C≡C absorption
choices.why: Both show it; the terminal alkyne's band is much more intense.

explanation: Alkynes show a C≡C stretching absorption at 2100 to 2260 cm^−1, an absorption that is much more intense for terminal alkynes than for internal alkynes.

prompt: Why is the ≡C–H stretching band at 3300 cm^−1 diagnostic for terminal alkynes?

choices.text: It is fairly intense and quite sharp
It is broad because of hydrogen bonding
choices.why: Broad bands caused by hydrogen bonding are typical of alcohol O–H groups.

choices.text: It lies in the fingerprint region, where few other bands appear
choices.why: 3300 cm^−1 is far above the fingerprint region, which is crowded with absorptions.

choices.text: Internal alkynes show it as well
choices.why: Only terminal alkynes have a ≡C–H bond.

explanation: Terminal alkynes such as 1-hexyne have a characteristic ≡C–H stretching absorption at 3300 cm^−1. This band is diagnostic for terminal alkynes because it is fairly intense and quite sharp.

prompt: Which set of IR absorptions is characteristic of an aromatic compound such as benzene?

choices.text: A weak C–H stretch at 3030 cm^−1, weak bands at 1660–2000 cm^−1 and medium bands at 1450–1600 cm^−1
A strong O–H band at 3400–3650 cm^−1, a C–O band at 1050–1150 cm^−1 and C–H bands at 2850–2960 cm^−1
choices.why: That set describes an alcohol.

choices.text: A sharp ≡C–H band at 3300 cm^−1, a C≡C band at 2100–2260 cm^−1 and C–H bands at 2850–2960 cm^−1
choices.why: That set describes a terminal alkyne.

choices.text: A strong C–H stretch at 3300 cm^−1, strong bands at 1660–2000 cm^−1 and weak bands at 1450–1600 cm^−1
choices.why: The positions and intensities are mixed up: aromatic C–H is weak at 3030 cm^−1, the 1660–2000 cm^−1 bands are weak, and the 1450–1600 cm^−1 bands are medium.

explanation: Aromatic compounds such as benzene have a weak C–H stretching absorption at 3030 cm^−1, just to the left of a typical saturated C–H band, a series of weak absorptions in the 1660 to 2000 cm^−1 range, and a series of medium-intensity absorptions in the 1450 to 1600 cm^−1 region from complex motions of the whole ring.

prompt: What can the C–H out-of-plane bending absorptions of a benzene derivative, between 650 and 1000 cm^−1, tell you?

choices.text: The substitution pattern of the ring
Whether the compound contains a carbonyl group
choices.why: A carbonyl group is identified by its sharp, intense band at 1670–1780 cm^−1.

choices.text: The molecular weight of the compound
choices.why: IR spectra don't give molecular weights; mass spectrometry does.

choices.text: Whether the ring carries an O–H group
choices.why: An O–H group shows up as a broad band at 3400–3650 cm^−1.

explanation: The C–H out-of-plane bending region for benzene derivatives, between 650 and 1000 cm^−1, gives valuable information about the ring's substitution pattern, just as the =C–H bending region does for alkenes.

prompt: Why is the O–H absorption band of an alcohol usually broad?

choices.text: Hydrogen bonding between O–H groups
The O–H group has a symmetric and an asymmetric stretch
choices.why: Two stretching modes explain the two N–H bands of primary amines, not the breadth of an O–H band.

choices.text: Ring strain stiffens the O–H bond
choices.why: Ring strain is discussed for the C=O bonds of cyclic ketones, not for O–H bands.

choices.text: The O–H bond is a double bond
choices.why: O–H is a single bond. Hydrogen bonding between O–H groups broadens its band.

explanation: Alcohols have a characteristic band in the range 3400 to 3650 cm^−1 that is usually broad and intense. Hydrogen bonding between O–H groups is responsible for making it so broad, and if an O–H stretch is present it's hard to miss.

prompt: Amines absorb at 3300–3500 cm^−1, in the same area as alcohols. How does an N–H band differ from an O–H band?

choices.text: The N–H band is much sharper and less intense
The N–H band is broader and more intense
choices.why: That is reversed. The broad, intense band is the alcohol O–H.

choices.text: The N–H band appears near 1715 cm^−1 instead
choices.why: N–H absorbs at 3300–3500 cm^−1; 1715 cm^−1 is where a ketone C=O absorbs.

choices.text: They look the same, so IR can't tell them apart
choices.why: The N–H band's sharper, weaker shape distinguishes it from an O–H band.

explanation: The N–H group of amines has a characteristic absorption in the 3300 to 3500 cm^−1 range. Although alcohols absorb in the same range, an N–H absorption band is much sharper and less intense than an O–H band.

prompt: An amine shows only one N–H stretching absorption in the 3300–3500 cm^−1 region. What kind of amine is it?

choices.text: A secondary amine, R2N–H
A primary amine, R–NH2
choices.why: Primary amines show two N–H absorptions, one for the symmetric and one for the asymmetric stretching mode.

choices.text: An alcohol, since amines don't absorb in this region
choices.why: Amines do absorb at 3300–3500 cm^−1, with a sharper band than an alcohol's O–H.

choices.text: An amine with two nitrogen atoms
choices.why: The number of N–H bands depends on whether one nitrogen carries one or two hydrogens, not on how many nitrogens there are.

explanation: Primary amines (R–NH2) have two N–H absorptions, one for the symmetric stretching mode and one for the asymmetric mode. Secondary amines (R2N–H) have only one N–H stretching absorption in this region.

prompt: How many N–H stretching absorptions does a primary amine, R–NH2, show in the 3300–3500 cm^−1 region?
explanation: Primary amines have two absorptions, one for the symmetric stretching mode and one for the asymmetric mode. Secondary amines (R2N–H) have only one.

prompt: Why are carbonyl groups the easiest functional groups to identify by IR spectroscopy?

choices.text: They give a sharp, intense peak in the range 1670–1780 cm^−1
They give a broad, intense band at 3400–3650 cm^−1
choices.why: That is the alcohol O–H band.

choices.text: They give several weak bands in the fingerprint region
choices.why: The carbonyl peak is sharp and intense and lies at 1670–1780 cm^−1, above the fingerprint region.

choices.text: Every kind of carbonyl compound absorbs at exactly the same wavenumber
choices.why: The exact position within the 1670–1780 cm^−1 range often tells you which kind of carbonyl group it is.

explanation: Carbonyl groups are the easiest to identify of all IR absorptions because of their sharp, intense peak in the range 1670 to 1780 cm^−1. The exact position within this range can often identify the kind of carbonyl group: aldehyde, ketone, ester and so forth.

prompt: At what wavenumber does the C=O of a saturated aldehyde absorb?
explanation: Saturated aldehydes absorb at 1730 cm^−1; aldehydes next to either a double bond or an aromatic ring absorb lower, at 1705 cm^−1.

prompt: At what wavenumber does the C=O of an aldehyde next to a double bond or an aromatic ring absorb?
explanation: Aldehydes next to either a double bond or an aromatic ring absorb at 1705 cm^−1, lower than saturated aldehydes at 1730 cm^−1.

prompt: Besides its C=O band, which absorption helps tell an aldehyde from a ketone?

choices.text: A weak C–H band at 2750 cm^−1
A broad O–H band at 3400–3650 cm^−1
choices.why: Neither aldehydes nor ketones have an O–H group.

choices.text: A C≡C band at 2100–2260 cm^−1
choices.why: That marks an alkyne, not a carbonyl compound.

choices.text: A C=C band near 1650 cm^−1
choices.why: That marks an alkene double bond.

explanation: The C–H group attached to the carbonyl is responsible for aldehyde absorptions at 2750 and 2850 cm^−1. They are not very intense, but the band at 2750 cm^−1 is helpful when trying to distinguish between an aldehyde and a ketone.

prompt: The C–H on an aldehyde's carbonyl carbon gives two absorptions. One is at 2750 cm^−1. At what wavenumber is the other?
explanation: The aldehyde C–H gives absorptions at 2750 and 2850 cm^−1. They aren't very intense, but the 2750 cm^−1 band helps distinguish an aldehyde from a ketone.

prompt: At what wavenumber do saturated open-chain ketones and six-membered cyclic ketones absorb?
explanation: Saturated open-chain ketones and six-membered cyclic ketones absorb at 1715 cm^−1. Ring strain in smaller rings raises the absorption.

prompt: At what wavenumber does the C=O of a five-membered cyclic ketone absorb?
explanation: Ring strain stiffens the C=O bond, so five-membered cyclic ketones absorb at 1750 cm^−1, above the 1715 cm^−1 of open-chain and six-membered cyclic ketones.

prompt: At what wavenumber does the C=O of a four-membered cyclic ketone absorb?
explanation: Four-membered cyclic ketones are even more strained and absorb at 1780 cm^−1, compared with 1750 cm^−1 for five-membered and 1715 cm^−1 for six-membered cyclic ketones.

prompt: How does ring strain affect the C=O absorption of a cyclic ketone?

choices.text: It stiffens the C=O bond, so smaller rings absorb at higher wavenumbers
It weakens the C=O bond, so smaller rings absorb at lower wavenumbers
choices.why: Ring strain stiffens the C=O bond, so five- and four-membered cyclic ketones absorb higher than open-chain ketones.

choices.text: It has no effect, since every ketone absorbs at the same wavenumber
choices.why: Five- and four-membered cyclic ketones absorb at higher wavenumbers than six-membered and open-chain ketones.

choices.text: It moves the C=O absorption into the fingerprint region
choices.why: The C=O band stays in the carbonyl range; ring strain shifts it upward.

explanation: Ring strain stiffens the C=O bond. Saturated open-chain and six-membered cyclic ketones absorb at the same position; five-membered cyclic ketones absorb higher, and four-membered cyclic ketones higher still.

prompt: At what wavenumber does the C=O of a saturated ester absorb?
explanation: Saturated esters have a C=O absorbance at 1735 cm^−1 and two strong absorbances in the 1300 to 1000 cm^−1 range from the C–O portion of the group.

prompt: At what wavenumber does the C=O of an ester next to an aromatic ring or a double bond absorb?
explanation: Like other carbonyl groups, esters next to either an aromatic ring or a double bond absorb lower, at 1715 cm^−1, about 20 to 30 cm^−1 below a saturated ester (1735 cm^−1).

prompt: Besides its C=O band, what else marks a saturated ester in the IR spectrum?

choices.text: Two strong C–O bands at 1300–1000 cm^−1
A broad O–H band at 2500–3100 cm^−1
choices.why: That is the O–H band of a carboxylic acid; an ester has no O–H group.

choices.text: Weak C–H bands at 2750 and 2850 cm^−1
choices.why: Those come from the hydrogen on an aldehyde's carbonyl carbon.

choices.text: A sharp N–H band at 3300–3500 cm^−1
choices.why: That is an amine N–H band.

explanation: Saturated esters have a C=O absorbance at 1735 cm^−1 and two strong absorbances in the 1300 to 1000 cm^−1 range from the C–O portion of the functional group.

prompt: 1-Cyclohexen-1-ylmethanol is a cyclohexene ring with a CH2OH group on one of the double-bond carbons. Which set of IR absorptions would you expect?

choices.why: This molecule has no triple bond and no carbonyl group.
The broad 2500–3100 cm^−1 O–H band and 1710 cm^−1 C=O belong to a carboxylic acid. This is an alcohol with no C=O.
There is no carbonyl group. The second functional group is a C=C double bond, which absorbs at 1640–1680 cm^−1.

explanation: Identify the functional groups and check Table 12.7.1. This molecule has an alcohol O–H group and an alkene double bond, so it absorbs at 3400–3650 cm^−1 (O–H), 3020–3100 cm^−1 (=C–H) and 1640–1680 cm^−1 (C=C) (Worked Example 12.8.1a).

prompt: The saturated methyl ester HC≡CCH2CH(CH3)CH2CO2CH3 also has a terminal alkyne. Which set of IR absorptions would you expect?

choices.why: Those are alkene bands, but this molecule has a triple bond.
An ester has no O–H group; it shows a C=O band at 1735 cm^−1.
There is no O–H group. The band near 3300 cm^−1 comes from the terminal ≡C–H.

explanation: This molecule has a terminal alkyne triple bond and a saturated ester carbonyl group, so it absorbs at 3300 cm^−1 (≡C–H), 2100–2260 cm^−1 (C≡C) and 1735 cm^−1 (C=O) (Worked Example 12.8.1b).

prompt: An unknown shows an intense IR absorption at 1725 cm^−1, a series of weak absorptions from 1800 to 2000 cm^−1, and a C–H absorption near 3030 cm^−1. Which compound fits?

choices.text: Phenylacetaldehyde, C6H5CH2CHO
Hexanal, CH3CH2CH2CH2CH2CHO
choices.why: Hexanal has a C=O group but no aromatic ring, so it wouldn't show the weak 1800–2000 cm^−1 bands or the aromatic C–H near 3030 cm^−1.

choices.text: Benzyl alcohol, C6H5CH2OH
choices.why: An alcohol would show a broad O–H band at 3400–3650 cm^−1 and no C=O band near 1725 cm^−1.

choices.text: Phenylacetylene, C6H5C≡CH
choices.why: It would show ≡C–H at 3300 cm^−1 and C≡C at 2100–2260 cm^−1, and it has no C=O to absorb at 1725 cm^−1.

explanation: The intense band at 1725 cm^−1 is a carbonyl group (perhaps an aldehyde, –CHO), and the weak bands from 1800 to 2000 cm^−1 and the C–H absorption near 3030 cm^−1 are characteristic of aromatic compounds. The compound is phenylacetaldehyde (Worked Example 12.8.2).

prompt: 2-(Hydroxymethyl)benzoic acid has a CO2H group and a CH2OH group on neighboring carbons of a benzene ring. Which O–H absorptions would you expect?

choices.text: 2500–3100 cm^−1 (broad, acid O–H) and 3400–3650 cm^−1 (alcohol O–H)
A single broad band at 3400–3650 cm^−1 shared by both O–H groups
choices.why: A carboxylic acid O–H absorbs at 2500–3100 cm^−1, separate from the alcohol O–H band.

choices.text: 2500–3100 cm^−1 (alcohol O–H) and 3400–3650 cm^−1 (acid O–H)
choices.why: That is reversed. The acid O–H is the 2500–3100 cm^−1 band; the alcohol O–H is at 3400–3650 cm^−1.

choices.text: Two sharp bands at 3300–3500 cm^−1, like a primary amine's
choices.why: Two sharp bands there mark a primary amine's NH2 group, and this molecule has no nitrogen.

explanation: Table 12.7.1 puts a carboxylic acid O–H at 2500–3100 cm^−1 (strong, broad) and an alcohol O–H at 3400–3650 cm^−1. The section's answer to Exercise 12.8.2c lists 1720 (C=O), 2500–3100 and 3400–3650 cm^−1.
